records.title: Online Peer-to-Peer Support for Young People With Mental Health Problems: A Systematic Review
records.design: systematic review (n=6 included studies)
records.population_setting: adolescents and young adults 12-25y, online peer-to-peer mental health support (Internet support groups, VR chat)
records.key_finding: 6 studies met inclusion criteria; peer support was moderated by health professionals, researchers, or consumers in almost all (5/6) studies; only 2 of 3 RCTs showed a significant positive outcome vs control, the other 4 studies found no effect.
records.relevance_to_tphe: complicates: mixed-to-weak effectiveness evidence for moderated peer support in this exact age band undercuts any claim Layer 3 will improve outcomes on its own; supports the design choice that moderation (not peer content alone) is the load-bearing safety feature, consistent with R4 routing.
records.evidence_level: systematic review of primary studies (small n, mixed designs)

records.title: Understanding the Impacts of Online Mental Health Peer Support Forums: Realist Synthesis
records.design: realist synthesis (102 evidence sources) + 18 stakeholder interviews with forum staff
records.population_setting: online mental health peer support forum users and staff, published 2019-2023
records.key_finding: Produced 22 context-mechanism-outcome configurations; psychological safety and content relevance drive engagement; moderators are described as vital to creating facilitative spaces and limiting distressing content; a key tension identified is balancing forum openness/anonymity against rule enforcement needed for community safety.
records.relevance_to_tphe: supports: directly parallels T-PHE Layer 3's design tension (anonymous, peer-governed R2 channel vs moderator enforcement of no-partner-visible-content rules) and names moderator role as the mechanism that makes such forums work, not the peer interaction alone.
records.evidence_level: realist synthesis (program theory, not effectiveness trial)

records.title: Understanding Safety in Online Mental Health Forums: Realist Evaluation
records.design: realist evaluation: 42 semistructured interviews + 504 cross-sectional survey responses
records.population_setting: users of 3 UK-based online mental health forums (general, young-people-focused, eating disorder/postpartum psychosis subforums)
records.key_finding: 40.1% agreed and 19.2% strongly agreed anonymity made them feel safe to post; but 18.8% agreed and 3.6% strongly agreed they had encountered distressing posts, and 22.4% agreed/3.4% strongly agreed that talking about mental health online could make them feel worse. Proactive content moderation and sensitive rule enforcement were identified as central safety mechanisms.
records.relevance_to_tphe: supports and complicates simultaneously: quantifies real harm rates (~20-26% distress-related concerns) alongside the anonymity-enables-disclosure mechanism T-PHE's Layer 3/R2 relies on; the coexistence of benefit and measurable harm argues for the routing-not-mediation moderator role (R4) rather than assuming anonymity alone is protective.
records.evidence_level: realist evaluation, single-country (UK), self-report survey plus qualitative interviews

records.title: Suicidal behaviours and moderator support in online health communities: a scoping review
records.design: scoping review (5 studies included after screening 397 records)
records.population_setting: online forum moderators supporting individuals experiencing suicidal behaviour
records.key_finding: Only 5 of 397 identified articles met inclusion criteria; only 1 article featured a moderator who was a qualified health professional, the rest were trained volunteers; evidence on moderators' professional working practices is described as sparse.
records.relevance_to_tphe: complicates: exposes a large evidence gap on what moderators actually do in crisis situations, directly relevant to whether T-PHE's Layer 3 moderators (non-clinical, volunteer-style per the proposal) can safely route acute-risk disclosures rather than mediate them; underscores need for explicit escalation protocols, not assumed competence.
records.evidence_level: scoping review (very small evidence base, moderate-quality primary studies)

records.title: Barriers and enablers to the moderation of self-harm content for a young person's online forum
records.design: qualitative interviews with 8 moderators (of 16 total) using the Behaviour Change Wheel
records.population_setting: moderators at The Mix, UK's leading online support service for people under 25
records.key_finding: Thematic analysis identified 11 enablers, 4 barriers, and 1 element that was both, to moderating self-harm content; barriers included emotional exhaustion, working with partial information, and vague guidelines; a 'moderation buddy' social-support strategy was proposed.
records.relevance_to_tphe: supports: directly informs the operational feasibility of T-PHE's moderator role for younger users; emotional exhaustion and vague guidelines are concrete implementation risks for a rule ('route, don't mediate') that this study shows is genuinely hard to apply consistently in practice.
records.evidence_level: qualitative study, single organisation (UK), n=8 moderators

records.title: The Role of Moderators in Facilitating and Encouraging Peer-to-Peer Support in an Online Mental Health Community: A Qualitative Exploratory Study
records.journal: Journal of Technology in Behavioral Science
records.design: qualitative thematic content analysis, interviews with 20 moderators
records.population_setting: moderators ('Wall Guides') of the Togetherall online peer support platform
records.key_finding: Moderators reported deep community connections and satisfaction from witnessing member progress, but also occasional aggressive, sensitive, or inconsiderate posts; response strategies included removing/revising posts, direct outreach to affected members, and consistent house-rule enforcement.
records.relevance_to_tphe: supports: an operating example of exactly the R4 'route, don't mediate' distinction in practice, with named response tactics (remove content, reach out to individual, enforce shared rules) that T-PHE's Layer 3 could model directly.
records.evidence_level: qualitative exploratory study, single platform, n=20 moderators

records.title: Safe spaces or toxic places? Content moderation and social dynamics of online eating disorder communities
records.design: comparative computational analysis: 2.6M tweets (Twitter/X), 178K submissions (Reddit), 14K videos (TikTok), 2019-2023
records.population_setting: online eating-disorder discussion communities across three major platforms
records.key_finding: Platforms with weaker moderation (Twitter/X) were found to enable toxic echo chambers that amplify pro-anorexia rhetoric, while more strongly moderated platforms did not show the same amplification pattern, despite similar user support-seeking behaviour across platforms.
records.relevance_to_tphe: contradicts/complicates: direct evidence that a peer community without robust, consistently enforced moderation can amplify harm rather than reduce it, which is a specific warning against under-resourcing the moderator function in T-PHE's Layer 3.
records.evidence_level: large-scale observational/computational content analysis (not causal experiment)

records.title: How Cancer Online Support Groups Work, for Whom, and in What Circumstances: Realist Review
records.design: realist review, 12 databases, 168 papers included from 16,659 identified
records.population_setting: patients with cancer and cancer survivors using online support groups (OSGs)
records.key_finding: OSGs can help via informational, emotional, appraisal, and altruistic support, but 'not all OSGs are helpful, and in some cases, they may increase distress'; positive outcomes depended on perceived trustworthiness, cultural safety, anonymity/privacy/control, and features such as moderation, norms, and group cohesion.
records.relevance_to_tphe: supports and complicates: the largest and most recent realist synthesis of any online peer support group in this search explicitly states outcomes are context-dependent and can be harmful, reinforcing that T-PHE cannot assume Layer 3 will help by default and must engineer for the named enabling conditions (trust, anonymity/control, active moderation).
records.evidence_level: realist review (high-volume evidence synthesis, non-RCT)

records.title: Online Social Support for Intimate Partner Violence Victims in China: Quantitative and Automatic Content Analysis
records.design: quantitative + automatic (machine-learning) content analysis of 90,040 messages (8,343 hand-coded subset)
records.population_setting: a popular Chinese online community's IPV discussion group
records.key_finding: Social support was commonly present in messages; only a small minority of messages expressed victim-blaming; the community functioned as a source of informational resources and emotional encouragement for IPV victims.
records.relevance_to_tphe: supports: empirical, non-Western evidence that a peer community around IPV/relationship harm can generate predominantly supportive (not blaming) content; the abstract does not state the community's moderation status, so no claim about being unmoderated-by-default is made. This is China-specific, offered only as a non-Western analogy - not evidence for a Thai or Muslim-majority setting.
records.evidence_level: observational content analysis, single platform/country, no outcome measure of victim wellbeing

records.title: Effectiveness of ICT-based intimate partner violence interventions: a systematic review
records.design: systematic review following PRISMA, 25 studies included
records.population_setting: women exposed to IPV, ICT-based interventions (internet, mobile, web, ehealth)
records.key_finding: ICT-based interventions were effective mainly for screening, disclosure, and prevention; the review found questions of safety, equity, and unintended consequences of ICT use in IPV programming were 'virtually non-existent' in the literature, and only one study formally assessed software usability.
records.relevance_to_tphe: complicates: a systematic review explicitly flags that safety/unintended-consequences research for digital IPV tools is almost absent, which is a direct evidence gap T-PHE's Layer 3 (a digital peer channel touching relationship-safety topics) would need to address rather than assume away.
records.evidence_level: systematic review (PRISMA), moderate methodological heterogeneity noted by authors

records.title: Intimate partner violence: a review of online interventions
records.design: scoping review, literature 2000-2016, 11 interventions identified
records.population_setting: women in the context of intimate partner violence, online interventions
records.key_finding: Existing online IPV interventions focused mainly on the act of leaving an abusive relationship, with limited emphasis on post-departure needs or the broader social-contextual factors of IPV; findings highlighted information gaps for women needing support after leaving.
records.relevance_to_tphe: complicates: suggests existing digital IPV support tools have a narrow scope (leaving-focused) that a peer community layer like T-PHE's would need to deliberately widen (post-separation, ongoing relationship-safety) rather than replicate the same gap.
records.evidence_level: scoping review, literature pre-2017 (dated relative to current social media landscape)

records.title: Technology-Facilitated Abuse in Intimate Relationships: A Scoping Review
records.design: scoping review, MEDLINE/CINAHL/Scopus, 22 studies (2000-2020), UK/Ireland/US/Canada/NZ/Australia
records.population_setting: adults 18+ in intimate partnerships experiencing technology-facilitated abuse (TFA)
records.key_finding: TFA is diverse and maps onto all eight domains of the Duluth Power & Control Wheel (surveillance apps, spyware, social media misuse etc.); impacts span social, mental-health, and financial harm plus a described sense of 'omnipresence'; victim/survivor resistance was infrequently reported and mainly involved direct action or professional/legal support.
records.relevance_to_tphe: supports the harms angle directly: names the specific mechanism by which a digital peer/relationship channel can itself become a vector of partner surveillance and control, which is exactly what T-PHE's 'no partner-visible content' rule (R2) is designed to defend against.
records.evidence_level: scoping review, English-speaking high-income countries only

records.title: Technology-Facilitated Domestic and Sexual Violence: A Review
records.design: narrative review
records.population_setting: adult women experiencing domestic and sexual violence via digital communications technologies
records.key_finding: Describes empirical literature on digital dating abuse, intimate partner cyberstalking, technology-facilitated sexual assault, image-based sexual abuse, and online sexual harassment as a growing, interconnected problem requiring gendered conceptual frameworks.
records.relevance_to_tphe: supports the harms angle: establishes that the same digital channels a peer-support layer would use (messaging, social platforms) are documented vectors for partner abuse, reinforcing the necessity of T-PHE's anonymous-by-choice and no-partner-visible-content design.
records.evidence_level: narrative review, non-systematic

records.title: Technology-Facilitated Domestic Violence Against Immigrant and Refugee Women: A Qualitative Study
records.design: qualitative study, interviews with 29 victim-survivors and 20 stakeholders
records.population_setting: immigrant and refugee women experiencing technology-facilitated domestic violence (TFDV), Australia
records.key_finding: Immigrant/refugee women face TFDV similarly to other women but with added unique barriers: language, cultural bias from services, limited financial resources, low trust in state institutions, and additional justice/migration-system obstacles.
records.relevance_to_tphe: complicates: raises a population-specific equity concern (migrant/minority status, language, institutional distrust) that a moderated digital peer community serving diverse Thai/Muslim populations should anticipate rather than assume uniform safety/trust across users.
records.evidence_level: qualitative study, single-country (Australia), not generalizable numerically

records.title: Cyberstalking Perpetrators and Their Methods: A Systematic Literature Review
records.design: systematic literature review, SCOPUS and Web of Science, 80 articles included
records.population_setting: cyberstalking perpetrators (general population studies)
records.key_finding: Perpetrators were characterised by poor social skills, low self-control, prior physical-abuse victimization, stalking-related attitudes, and higher internet use; common motives were relationship reconciliation, revenge, or establishing control; most frequent methods were unwanted repeated contact, account access, GPS tracking, and impersonation online.
records.relevance_to_tphe: supports the harms angle: names concrete cyberstalking methods (account access, GPS tracking, impersonation, unwanted contact via the same platforms) directly relevant to why T-PHE's Layer 3 must be designed so a partner cannot surveil or access a learner's peer-community activity.
records.evidence_level: systematic review, mixed empirical study designs and quality

records.title: Post-separation Parenting Apps as Tools for Control and Resistance
records.design: qualitative study, interviews with 18 separated mothers
records.population_setting: mothers coparenting post-separation with a domestic-violence perpetrator, using court-recommended communication apps
records.key_finding: Record-keeping functions built into coparenting apps (intended for accountability) were shown to function as sites where coercive control is both exercised and resisted, shaped by the legal context that mandated the apps' use.
records.relevance_to_tphe: complicates: a cautionary parallel showing that a technology explicitly designed to be safe/accountable can still be repurposed for control by an abusive partner, a direct design-risk lesson for any T-PHE feature (records, logs) touching relationship communication.
records.evidence_level: qualitative study, small sample (n=18), single-country context

records.title: Self-disclosure versus self-presentation on social media
records.design: narrative review of the literature on medium characteristics and online self-disclosure
records.population_setting: general social media users
records.key_finding: Anonymity and reduced information richness were identified as factors that increase self-disclosure, while asynchronicity, multiple audiences, and audience feedback were identified as factors favoring self-presentation (impression management) instead of genuine disclosure.
records.relevance_to_tphe: complicates: identifies structural features of online spaces (audience visibility, feedback dynamics) that can push users toward curated self-presentation rather than honest disclosure, a caveat for assuming anonymity alone in T-PHE's Layer 3 guarantees candid peer consultation.
records.evidence_level: narrative review, non-systematic, theoretical synthesis

records.title: Disclosure in psychotherapy versus in anonymous and non-anonymous online spaces
records.design: cross-sectional online survey, N=443
records.population_setting: heterogeneous adult sample comparing disclosure in therapy vs. anonymous/non-anonymous online spaces
records.key_finding: Attachment style significantly predicted likelihood of disclosing distressing topics online and whether disclosures in therapy vs. anonymous/non-anonymous online spaces were experienced as helpful; clinicians are advised to monitor whether younger patients and those with avoidant/ambivalent attachment styles view psychotherapy itself as an appropriate venue for disclosure, given their documented tendency to disclose online instead.
records.relevance_to_tphe: supports and complicates: gives an individual-differences mechanism (attachment style) for why 'younger people treat digital spaces as safer' is not uniformly true, and flags that clinicians should monitor whether such patients still see psychotherapy (the professional venue) as legitimate, given their tendency to disclose online instead - by extension a caution for T-PHE's moderators not to assume online disclosure substitutes for professional venues.
records.evidence_level: cross-sectional survey study, correlational, self-report

records.title: Young People's Online Help-Seeking and Mental Health Difficulties: Systematic Narrative Review
records.design: systematic narrative review (PRISMA), 28 studies included
records.population_setting: young people seeking help online for mental health difficulties
records.key_finding: Key benefits of online help-seeking were anonymity/privacy, immediacy, ease of access, inclusivity, connection with others, and greater sense of control; barriers included low mental health literacy, privacy/confidentiality concerns, and uncertainty about trustworthiness of online resources; limited theoretical frameworks have been applied to online help-seeking.
records.relevance_to_tphe: supports: the closest direct evidence for the proposal's stated assumption that younger people find digital spaces safer/more accessible for help-seeking, while also naming trust/credibility barriers relevant to how T-PHE's Layer 3 should be governed and presented.
records.evidence_level: systematic narrative review (PRISMA), moderate-to-strong quality primary studies

records.title: Social Media and Online Digital Technology Use Among Muslim Young People and Parents: Qualitative Focus Group Study
records.design: qualitative participatory study, focus groups with 33 young people (16-22y) and 15 parents (40-57y)
records.population_setting: Muslim young people and parents, Melbourne, Australia
records.key_finding: Social media served as an important extension of social/cultural/religious connection, especially during COVID-19; young participants used it to build identity and belonging, but also faced discrimination and unrealistic beauty/success standards online; a large digital divide existed between young people's and parents' online experiences and concerns.
records.relevance_to_tphe: supports and complicates: the only Muslim-community-specific record found; supports that digital spaces can serve identity/belonging/community-connection functions relevant to T-PHE's target population, but also documents discrimination exposure as a harm and a parent-youth digital-divide relevant to family-context governance of Layer 3.
records.evidence_level: qualitative focus-group study, single city/country, not Thailand-specific

gaps_noted: No PubMed-indexed record was found specific to Thailand, or to a Thai Muslim population, on digital peer support, online IPV support, or moderated online communities; the Muslim-specific record found (PMID 35536616) is set in Australia, and other Muslim/health hits from the search (PMID 37928060 anti-Muslim discrimination, PMID 38040423 Sikh/Muslim kidney transplant views, PMID 31120322 US Muslim contraceptive beliefs) were off-angle and excluded.

No PubMed-indexed record evaluates a premarital-education-linked or nikah/marriage-preparation digital peer community anywhere; this proposal's Layer 3 model appears untested in the indexed literature.

Evidence on moderator training, competence, and error rates in routing acute-risk disclosures (self-harm, IPV, abuse) to services is sparse (PMID 34193497 found only 5 usable studies after screening 397); no record quantifies false-negative or delayed-routing rates for non-clinical moderators.

No LMIC/Southeast Asia-specific systematic review of moderated digital peer support for relationship or premarital health topics was found via this angle; the closest LMIC-adjacent records (PMID 37540713, 38558241, 39116286) concern general digital health promotion, not peer community moderation specifically, and were excluded as off-angle.

Evidence quantifying how often anonymity itself is defeated by partner technology-facilitated surveillance of a specific digital peer-support platform (as opposed to general social media/apps) was not found; existing TFA evidence (PMID 35537445, 32998673, 40271872) describes general digital abuse mechanisms, not platform-specific breach of anonymous peer-support spaces.
limits_of_this_search: Restricted to PubMed-indexed records retrievable via NCBI E-utilities esearch/efetch with title/abstract-field queries; grey literature, non-indexed platform-safety reports, and non-English-language studies (e.g., Thai-language journals not in PubMed) were not searched. Seven queries were run and abstracts read for 20 selected records out of 98 unique candidate PMIDs identified; record selection was investigator-judged for angle relevance, not a formal systematic-review screening process, so this is a scoping literature snapshot, not a systematic review. No study directly tests a peer community structurally identical to T-PHE's proposed Layer 3, so all relevance judgments are by analogy to structurally similar online peer-support, IPV-support, or technology-facilitated-abuse literature.
